concept.name: Total return swap
concept.definition: A swap in which one party (the total return payer) transfers the full economic performance of a reference asset — its income plus any price appreciation or depreciation — to the other party, which in return pays a financing rate (a reference rate plus a spread) on the notional. It transfers the asset's returns without transferring ownership and is classed among the common credit derivatives.
concept.intuition: A total return swap lets you collect everything a stock, bond, or index pays and earns — as if you owned it — while posting only a fraction of its value as margin and paying a financing charge.
concept.mechanics: On each payment date the payer passes through coupons or dividends plus the mark-to-market change in the reference asset; if the asset fell, the receiver pays the loss. The receiver thus holds leveraged synthetic exposure, while the payer (often a dealer that owns or hedges the asset) sheds its price risk.
concept.formula: Total return payment = income received on the reference asset + (P_end - P_start) x notional quantity; financing leg = notional x (reference rate + spread) x day-count fraction.
concept.failure_modes: The receiver bears the full downside of the reference asset plus counterparty risk, and the embedded leverage is largely invisible on the balance sheet — the 2021 Archegos collapse was built on equity total return swaps. Financing spreads can also widen or financing be withdrawn in stress.
concept.misconceptions: That receiving total return confers shareholder rights — it transfers economics only, not voting or ownership. Also, dealers are not betting against the client by default; they typically hedge the reference asset.
concept.example: A fund receives the total return on $50 million notional of an equity basket and pays SOFR plus 60 basis points quarterly; a 4% rise in the basket over a quarter nets it roughly $2 million minus financing.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
